ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, it is known that point $D$ lies on the extension of the diameter $AB$ of circle $O$, and point $C$ lies on circle $O$. A line is drawn through $D$ perpendicular to $AD$ and intersects with the extension of $AC$ at $E$. $CD$ is a tangent to circle $O$; $AB=2$ and $AE=3$. $CD=DE$; find the length of $BD$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Method One: \\
Since $AB=2$, \\
it follows that $OA=OB=OC=1$, \\
Since $OC\perp CD$, \\
by the Pythagorean theorem, we have $CD^{2}=(1+BD)^{2}-1^{2}$, \\
Since $ED\perp AD$, \\
by the Pythagorean theorem, we have $DE^{2}=3^{2}-(2+BD)^{2}$, \\
Since $CD=DE$, \\
it follows that $(1+BD)^{2}-1^{2}=3^{2}-(2+BD)^{2}$, \\
Solving this gives: $BD=\frac{-3+\sqrt{19}}{2}$ or $\frac{-3-\sqrt{19}}{2}$ (discard this result),\\
thus $BD=\boxed{\frac{-3+\sqrt{19}}{2}}$. \\

Method Two: \\
By the chord tangent theorem, we have $\angle DCB=\angle DAC$, \\
Since $\angle CDB=\angle ADC$, \\
it follows that $\triangle CDB\sim \triangle ADC$, \\
hence $\frac{CD}{AD}=\frac{BD}{CD}$, that is, $CD^{2}=AD\cdot BD=(2+BD)\cdot BD$, \\
Since $ED\perp AD$, \\
by the Pythagorean theorem, we have $DE^{2}=3^{2}-(2+BD)^{2}$, \\
Since $CD=DE$, \\
it follows that $(2+BD)\times BD=3^{2}-(2+BD)^{2}$, \\
Solving this gives $BD=\frac{-3+\sqrt{19}}{2}$ or $\frac{-3-\sqrt{19}}{2}$ (discard this result),\\
thus $BD=\boxed{\frac{-3+\sqrt{19}}{2}}$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there is a circle, AB is a horizontal diameter, and O is on AB as the center of the circle; D is located to the right of B, on the extension line of diameter AB; C is on the circumference at the upper right of the circle; line AC continues to extend to E at the upper right; the vertical line segment DE drawn through D is perpendicular to the horizontal line AD; the figure also connects C to D, and the problem statement says that CD is a tangent to circle O, and gives AB=2, AE=3, CD=DE.
